3. **On macOS the two paths are the same file.** The write lands in place, `git status` reports *no change*, and `browser_export.py` sees one file. Every local gate passes.
4. **On Linux CI, git checks out the capital-P file and the exporter creates the lowercase-p one.** Now there are two. `browser_export.py` reads 2842 records against a `docs/data/` carrying 2841, and `check_flat_export_coverage` correctly reports `ingredients.json` stale.

The published artifact was never wrong. The *tracked filename* was — and nothing on a macOS checkout can tell you.

## Why the existing guards miss it

- `git status` — clean, because the filesystem folds the case.
- `check_flat_export_coverage` — passes locally, because the exporter and the checker both see the same single file.
- `verify_roundtrip` — passes, because the record content is fine.

The failure only materialises where the filesystem is case-sensitive, i.e. only in CI, with an error message pointing at `ingredients.json` rather than at the filename that actually moved.

## Suggested guard

A check that compares `git ls-files data/ingredients` against the names the exporter *would* write, **case-sensitively**, and fails on any pair differing only by case. That is computable on any platform without needing a case-sensitive volume:

```python
tracked = {p.rsplit('/', 1)[-1] for p in git_ls_files('data/ingredients')}
collisions = [n for n in tracked if n.lower() in {t.lower() for t in tracked} - {n.lower()} ]
# plus: for each record, assert the exporter's target name is the tracked name, byte for byte
```

Note the naive version of this is not enough — the exporter's collision handling depends on what is already in the output directory, so exporting into an empty temp dir produces *different* names than exporting in place (~1150 differ). The check has to compare against an in-place export, or the exporter's naming has to be made independent of existing directory contents, which would be the better fix.

## Prior occurrence

The same class caused an apparent record loss earlier (`Sodium_Tartrate` vs `Sodium_tartrate`), where the count dropped by one on export and the shared-identifier path was initially blamed.
title: A record filename whose case changes is invisible on macOS and breaks CI on Linux

body:
Found during the #320 triage.

A live record has `preferred_term: "D"` — a single character — mapped to `CHEBI:29958 L-aspartic acid residue`, and carried `cas_rn: 138-86-3`, which is **limonene**.

Three fields, three different substances implied:

| field | value | denotes |
|---|---|---|
| `preferred_term` | `D` | nothing determinate |
| `ontology_id` | `CHEBI:29958` | L-aspartic acid *residue* (a polymer residue, not a free compound) |
| `cas_rn` | `138-86-3` | limonene |

The CAS was withdrawn in #345 as demonstrably false, but that is the smallest problem here. Two structural issues remain:

1. **The label is almost certainly a parsing artifact.** A single `D` suggests a truncated or mis-split field upstream — a one-letter amino-acid code, a column shift, or a stray token from a recipe table. Which of those it is determines whether the record should be relabelled, merged, or deleted.
2. **`CHEBI:29958` is a residue term, not a substance term.** Residue classes describe a unit *within* a polymer and should generally not be the mapping target for a growth-medium ingredient at all, independent of what the label turns out to mean. Worth checking whether other records are also grounded to `...residue` terms.

Resolving this needs the upstream source row (which recipe, which column), not chemistry — so it is filed rather than guessed at. If the source cannot be recovered, the honest outcome is to tombstone the record rather than leave three mutually contradictory fields published.
title: Record `D`: single-character label mapped to an amino-acid residue

body:
Found during the adversarial review of #341, by checking each label's stated hydration number against the known stable hydrates of that salt.

| record label | stated n | known hydrates |
|---|---|---|
| `CaCl2 x 7 H2O` | 7 | 1, 2, 4, 6 |
| `CuCl2 x 6 H2O` | 6 | 2 |
| `FeCl2 x 6 H2O` | 6 | 2, 4 |
| `FeCl2 x 7 H2O` | 7 | 2, 4 |
| `FeCl3 x 4 H2O` | 4 | 6 |
| `MgCl2 x 7 H2O` | 7 | 6 |
| `Na2HPO4 x 3 H2O` | 3 | 2, 7, 8, 12 |
| `Na2HPO4 x 6 H2O` | 6 | 2, 7, 8, 12 |
| `NiCl2 x 5 H2O` | 5 | 2, 4, 6 |

10 of the 19 checked do match a known hydrate, so this is not a systematic notation problem — it is 9 specific labels.

## The pattern worth chasing first

`MgCl2 x 7 H2O` and `FeCl2 x 7 H2O` stand out: **`MgSO4·7H2O` and `FeSO4·7H2O` are among the most common salts in microbial growth media**, and both are genuine heptahydrates. A sulfate → chloride slip somewhere upstream would produce exactly these two labels. Worth checking the source rows before assuming the hydration number is what's wrong — it may be the anion.

Note MIM already holds separate `FeSO4 x 7 H2O` records (`CHEBI:75832`/`CHEBI:75836` appear as a same-name-different-identifier pair in the duplicate report), so a comparison against those recipes is possible.

## Relationship to #341

#341 corrected these records' `molecular_formula` from the anhydrous salt's to one that includes the stated water, so for these 9 the formula now faithfully encodes a hydration number that may not correspond to a real substance. That is **not a regression** — the previous value (the anhydrous formula) was wrong for every hydrate — but it does mean the formula is only as good as the label, and these 9 labels are in question.

Resolving this needs the upstream source rows (MediaDive / CultureBotHT / the original recipe text), not chemistry reasoning, so it was filed rather than guessed at.
title: 9 hydrate labels state a hydration number with no known corresponding hydrate

body:
`tests/test_check_chebi_currency.py::test_kgmicrobe_default_is_a_sibling_not_a_hardcoded_home` fails on the untouched tree, reproducible on `main`:

```
assert "/Users/" not in str(mod.default_kgm_chebi())
E  AssertionError: assert '/Users/' not in '/Users/marcin/.../kg-microbe/data/raw/chebi.owl.gz'
```

The test was written to catch a **hardcoded** home directory. It asserts the absence of the literal `/Users/`, but this repo genuinely lives under `/Users/<name>/` on macOS, so a *correctly computed sibling path* trips it too. The assertion cannot distinguish the bug it targets from the correct behaviour on the platform most likely to exhibit either.

It passes in CI only because CI runs on Linux (`/home/runner`), so the check is a permanent no-op there — the opposite of what it was written for, and it fails for every macOS developer.

Suggested fix: assert the property directly rather than via a substring — e.g. that the path is a sibling of the repo root (`default_kgm_chebi()` is relative to `ROOT.parent`), or that it does not contain a home directory *other than* the current user's. Comparing against `Path.home()` would keep the original intent without the platform false positive.

Found during the adversarial review of #341; unrelated to that PR's changes.
title: test_check_chebi_currency fails on any macOS checkout under /Users

body:
Found during the adversarial review of #341.

50 records assert `skos:narrowMatch` from a hydrate to its **anhydrous** form (22 from the earlier `anchor_cas_hydrate_records` cohort, 28 from #341). `narrowMatch` asserts the subject is *more specific than* the object — i.e. a subsumption.

**ChEBI denies that subsumption.** Querying `chebi.db`:

| hydrate | direct parents | anhydrous form an ancestor? |
|---|---|---|
| `CHEBI:53503` cobalt chloride hexahydrate | `CHEBI:35505 hydrate` | **no** (`CHEBI:35696`) |
| `CHEBI:53542` nickel chloride hexahydrate | `CHEBI:35505 hydrate` | **no** (`CHEBI:34887`) |
| `CHEBI:91258` disodium hydrogenphosphate dihydrate | `CHEBI:35505 hydrate` | **no** (`CHEBI:34683`) |
| `CHEBI:86345` magnesium dichloride hexahydrate | `CHEBI:35505 hydrate`, `CHEBI:36093`, `CHEBI:51234` | **no** (`CHEBI:6636`) |

ChEBI files hydrates under `CHEBI:35505 hydrate`, never under the anhydrous compound. Chemically that is the right call: `CoCl2·2H2O` is a distinct substance that *contains* `CoCl2`, not a specialization of it — it has a different formula, mass, crystal structure and CAS.

## Why this wasn't changed in #341

The convention is unanimous across all 22 pre-existing records, so flipping 28 of 50 would have left the corpus internally inconsistent, and the predicate choice is a semantics decision rather than a defect fix. #341 is still a strict improvement on those 28: they previously asserted `skos:exactMatch` (identity **with the anhydrous salt**), which is unambiguously worse.

## The decision

Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. **`skos:closeMatch`** — honest about "same compound, different hydration state", no subsumption claim. Note this changes Rule B1's reach: B1 only requires a registry row for narrow/broadMatch, so these subjects would stop being covered by it even though the minted `kgmicrobe.compound:` identity row is still correct and should stay.
2. **`skos:relatedMatch`** — weaker, arguably too weak to be useful downstream.
3. **Keep `narrowMatch`** and document in `MAPPING_SEMANTICS` that MIM reads it as "more specific *form* of", not strict subsumption — cheapest, but overloads a predicate with a defined meaning.

Whichever is chosen should be applied to all 50 at once and written into `MAPPING_SEMANTICS` §3 so the next hydrate cohort doesn't re-litigate it.
title: narrowMatch for hydrate → anhydrous contradicts ChEBI's own hierarchy (50 records)

body:
Found in review of #326a (PR below). Pre-existing — the count is identical on
`origin/main` and on the branch, so nothing here introduced it.

## The gap

`reconcile_sssom.PREDICATE` defines the mapping:

```
EXACT_MATCH   -> skos:exactMatch      NARROW_MATCH -> skos:narrowMatch
SYNONYM_MATCH -> skos:exactMatch      BROAD_MATCH  -> skos:broadMatch
CLOSE_MATCH   -> skos:closeMatch
```

**55 published rows disagree with the record they describe.** All in the same
direction: the record says `EXACT_MATCH`/`SYNONYM_MATCH` while the row says
`skos:closeMatch`.

```
AlCl3             EXACT_MATCH    row: skos:closeMatch
AlK(SO4)2         EXACT_MATCH    row: skos:closeMatch
Arsenate          SYNONYM_MATCH  row: skos:closeMatch
beta-NAD          EXACT_MATCH    row: skos:closeMatch
BICINE buffer     EXACT_MATCH    row: skos:closeMatch
CaCl2             EXACT_MATCH    row: skos:closeMatch
Calcium Chloride  SYNONYM_MATCH  row: skos:closeMatch
CaSO4             EXACT_MATCH    row: skos:closeMatch
…
```

## Why nothing caught it

`reconcile_sssom` compares **object ids** — it reports GAP (record with no row),
ORPHAN (row with no record) and STALE (row not pointing at the record's current
`ontology_id`). A row pointing at the right object with the *wrong predicate* is
none of those, so it passes cleanly. `check_flat_export_coverage` is about label
resolvability and does not look at predicates either.

The direction matters: the records claim identity while the published mappings
claim only a close match. Downstream, `skos:closeMatch` does not license the
node substitution `skos:exactMatch` does — so consumers are getting a weaker
assertion than the curation says. That is the safe direction to be wrong in, but
it means the SSSOM understates 55 curated identities.

## Suggested action

Add a predicate-consistency check to `reconcile_sssom` alongside GAP/ORPHAN/STALE
— it is a dict lookup against a table the script already defines — then reconcile
the 55. Worth deciding first whether the row or the record is authoritative:
these look like records that were re-graded upward at some point without the row
following, which would make the record right.

Reproduction: for each SSSOM row whose `object_id` equals the record's
`ontology_mapping.ontology_id`, compare `predicate_id` against
`PREDICATE[mapping_quality]`.
title: 55 SSSOM rows carry a predicate that contradicts the record's mapping_quality

body:
Found while working #321. Two findings, both beyond what that issue describes.

## 1. The worst collapses are duplicates, not just mis-mappings

`CoCl2 x 6 H2O` sits on the **anhydrous** term `CHEBI:35696` — while a sibling
record already holds the correct one:

```
CHEBI:35696  CoCl2 x 6 H2O                     <- anhydrous term
CHEBI:53503  Cobalt chloride hexahydrate       occ=123, CAS 7791-13-1, correct
```

Same for nickel: `NiCl2 x 6 H2O` on `CHEBI:34887` while
`Nickel (II) chloride hexahydrate` (occ=122) correctly holds `CHEBI:53542`.

This is the `Ca-pantothenate` shape from #315 — a notation the merge pass does
not recognise as naming the same substance (`Ca-` vs `Calcium …`, here
`CoCl2 x 6 H2O` vs `Cobalt chloride hexahydrate`). Having escaped the merge, the
survivor was then grounded to the nearest thing lexical matching could find: the
anhydrous parent.

So the remedy for those two is a **merge**, not a promotion — and a promotion
would have failed anyway, because the target identifier is already taken.
Worth adding formula-notation ↔ spelled-out equivalence to the duplicate
normaliser, alongside the `Ca-`/`Na-` prefix expansion #315 suggested.

## 2. CAS numbers are scrambled within each hydrate family

Independently of the mapping, the `cas_rn` values are close to arbitrary:

```
CoCl2, CoCl2 x 2 H2O, x 4 H2O, x 6 H2O   ALL carry 7646-79-9  (the anhydrous CAS)
NiCl2 x 2 H2O, NiCl2 x 5 H2O             both carry 7791-20-0 (the HEXAhydrate CAS)
NiCl2 x 6 H2O                            carries 7718-54-9    (the anhydrous CAS)
Na2HPO4 x 2 H2O                          carries 7558-79-4    (anhydrous; the dihydrate is 10028-24-7)
Na2HPO4 x 3/6/7/12 H2O                   all carry 7782-85-6
```

ChEBI's own xrefs give the right values — `CHEBI:91258` (dihydrate) →
`cas:10028-24-7`, `CHEBI:53542` (nickel hexahydrate) → `cas:7791-20-0` — so the
correct CAS for a hydrate is recoverable wherever a specific term exists.

Note the interaction: `7791-20-0` is *currently* on the di- and pentahydrate
records and *belongs* to the hexahydrate. Any CAS-keyed dedup or join run today
would merge the wrong records.

## Scope

`#321`'s 39 records include 4 terms absorbing 13 records. Of those 13, ChEBI has
a specific term for exactly 4:

| record | target | action |
|---|---|---|
| `Na2HPO4 x 2 H2O` | CHEBI:91258 | promote (free) |
| `Na2HPO4 x 12 H2O` | CHEBI:91259 | promote (free) |
| `CoCl2 x 6 H2O` | CHEBI:53503 | **merge** (taken) |
| `NiCl2 x 6 H2O` | CHEBI:53542 | **merge** (taken) |

The remaining 9 (`Na2HPO4 x 3/6/7`, `CoCl2 x 2/4`, `NiCl2 x 2/5`, `FeCl2 x 6/7`)
have no ChEBI term and no trustworthy CAS, so they need §3 step 2 with a
*verified* CAS or step 3, per record. Not attempted blind.
title: Hydrate collapse is partly a duplicate problem: formula-notation labels shadow correctly-mapped siblings

body:
Self-review finding on the #323 classifier (PR #328), before it merges.

## The defect

The classifier has three rule families. Two are sound; one is not.

| rule | assigned | reliability |
|---|---|---|
| chemical namespace / structure (CHEBI-with-structure, `cas:`) | 422 | sound |
| **name pattern** (`serum`, `agar`, `digest`, `solution`, …) | 15 | sound |
| **biological namespace** (FOODON / MICRO / BTO / ENVO primary → UNDEFINED_MIXTURE) | **10** | **~25% wrong** |

The namespace rule infers "this is an undefined mixture" from *which ontology
happened to have a term*, which is not the same question. Wrong on inspection:

- **`Carboxymethyl cellulose (sodium salt)`** → UNDEFINED_MIXTURE because it is
  FOODON-primary. CMC sodium is a **defined polymer**; the research lane
  separately recommended `NCIT:C83596 Carboxymethylcellulose Sodium` for it. A
  degree-of-substitution range does not make it an undefined mixture.
- **`Bovine albumin`** → UNDEFINED_MIXTURE because MICRO-primary. BSA is a
  purified protein. (Fraction V preparations are heterogeneous, so this one is
  arguable — but it is being decided by namespace, not by that argument.)

Also questionable, from the *name* family rather than the namespace one:

- **`Bile Acid`** → UNDEFINED_MIXTURE on the word `bile`. Bile acids are a
  **class of steroid acids**, not an undefined biological mixture the way
  `Bile salts` or `Horse serum` is. The pattern is right for the others and
  wrong here.

## Why it matters more than 10 records

`ingredient_type` exists to tell an enrichment pass which empty
`chemical_properties` are legitimately empty (#316). Marking a defined polymer
UNDEFINED_MIXTURE tells every future pass **not** to enrich a record that could
be enriched — a silent, permanent exclusion, and the exact failure mode this
field was introduced to prevent, pointed the other way.

## Recommendation

Apply the classifier's own stated principle — *a wrong value is worse than an
absent one* — to the rule that does not meet it: **drop the biological-namespace
inference and leave those 10 unset**, alongside the 109 already left for review.
A curator seeing "unset, FOODON primary" will make a better call than the rule
does.

The name-pattern rule stays; `Bile Acid` is a single-record exception to note,
not a reason to drop it.

That takes PR #328 from 447 assigned / 109 unset to **437 assigned / 119 unset**,
and removes the only rule family with a measurable error rate.
title: ingredient_type: the biological-namespace rule mis-classifies defined substances

body:
## The check

A `narrowMatch`/`closeMatch` asserts the record is *more specific* than the term.
If the record's `molecular_formula` is **identical** to the term's own formula,
one of the two is wrong. No external lookup — both values are already local.

**36 records.** They split cleanly, with opposite fixes.

## (a) 24 — the same substance, so the grade is wrong

Different naming convention, not different chemistry. `narrowMatch` should be
exact/synonym:

| record | term |
|---|---|
| `4'-Methoxyflavone` | `2-(4-methoxyphenyl)-1-benzopyran-4-one` |
| `1,4-B-D-Galactobiose` | `beta-D-galactopyranosyl-(1->4)-D-galactopyranose` |
| `6-Pentyl-2H-pyran-2-one` | `6-n-Pentyl-alpha-pyrone` |
| `L-Meta-tyrosine` | `L-m-tyrosine` |
| `Gly-DL-Asp` | `Glycyl-Aspartate` |
| `3'-fucosyllactose` | `3-fucosyllactose` |

Two of these — `4'-Methoxyflavone` and `1,4-B-D-Galactobiose` — were found
independently, one record at a time, by the research lane, which called both
"an exact match mis-filed as a parent". The mechanical check reproduces them and
finds 22 more.

Root cause is visible in their histories: `BACKFILL_PARENT_CHEBI` located the
term via a PubChem xref and filed it as a *parent*. A "parent" with an identical
formula and mass is not a parent.

## (b) 12 — the formula was inherited from the parent and is factually wrong

Here the `narrowMatch` is **correct** — the label names a salt or hydrate, which
genuinely is narrower. The defect is that `molecular_formula` was backfilled
from the parent, so the record publishes the *parent's* formula:

```
Betaine hydrochloride        C5H11NO2   <- glycine betaine's. The HCl salt is C5H12ClNO2.
D-Galacturonic Acid monohydrate         <- anhydrous formula, no water
Vancomycin Hydrochloride Hydrate        <- parent's
Sodium hypophosphite monohydrate        <- parent's
Carnitine (Dl) Hydrochloride            <- parent's
… 2-Deoxy-D-ribonic acid lithium salt, D-xylose 5-phosphate lithium salt,
  sn-Glycerol 3-phosphate lithium salt, Nitrilotriacetic acid disodium salt,
  Polygalacturonic acid sodium salt, Gly-Gln monohydrate, Stachyose hydrate
```

This is exactly what `MAPPING_SEMANTICS` §3 warns about — *"Do not treat a
record's auto-derived chemistry as evidence of its identity"* — caught in the
act. Four of the twelve are also #321 hydrates, found by an independent route,
which is useful corroboration for both.

**Fixing (b) by re-grading would be wrong**, and vice versa. The discriminator
is whether the label carries a salt/hydrate qualifier.

## Suggested action

- (a): re-grade to exact/synonym per #317's procedure, after confirming identity
  by InChIKey rather than by formula alone (formula equality is necessary, not
  sufficient — `Fructooligosaccharides (FOS)` matches `beta-D-fructofuranose`
  on C6H12O6 and is a polymer mixture, so it belongs in neither group).
- (b): clear the inherited `molecular_formula` — do **not** replace it from the
  same source that produced it.
- Add the check as a standing gate; it is local and cheap.

## Provenance

Surfaced when the field-name bug behind #321 was fixed. This check was reported
on #324 as finding "0 hits" — it was reading `chemical_properties.formula`,
which does not exist (the field is `molecular_formula`), so it compared `None`
against every parent and matched nothing.

Related: #317, #320, #321, #324.
title: 36 records whose NARROW_MATCH parent has an identical molecular formula

body:
## The defect

`cas:71592-46-6` `3',6-Dihydroxyflavone` → `CHEBI:107657`
**`6-methoxy-2-(3-methoxyphenyl)-1-benzopyran-4-one`**

The label says **dihydroxy**. The CAS, formula, SMILES, InChI, PubChem CID and
the cited CHEBI term all say **dimethoxy** — C17H14O4 against C15H10O4, a
difference of two methyls (+28.05 Da). PubChem CID 676293's own synonym array
contains both `6,3'-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE` and the literal string `71592-46-6`.

The compound the label names is real (CID 688662) and has **no ChEBI term**.

## Why this is the worst shape of defect

**It is internally self-consistent.** The CAS→structure round trip closes; the
formula matches the SMILES; the InChIKey matches PubChem. Every check that
compares the record's chemistry fields against each other passes. Only
**label vs structure** disagrees — and nothing was comparing those.

That also means it is invisible to the checks already deployed: #320 (CAS
registered against a different term) passes, and the CAS-vs-InChIKey audit
passes.

## Two proposed detectors, with honest precision

**(a) Label vs PubChem Title, for `cas:`-primary records.** One lookup per
record: resolve the CAS and compare the returned Title to `preferred_term`.
Here: Title `6,3'-Dimethoxyflavone` vs label `3',6-Dihydroxyflavone` → mismatch.
It discriminates rather than flagging everything — the other nine records in the
batch it came from all pass. 256 `cas:`-primary records, so this is feasible but
needs network calls.

**(b) A purely local approximation — label vs `ontology_label` substituent
classes.** Cheap, no lookups, but I ran it and it is **not** reliable enough to
deploy as-is: 3 hits, 1 true positive (this record) and 2 false positives —
`methylene chloride` → `dichloromethane` (the same substance; "chloride" does
not match a `chloro` pattern) and `Dimethylfraxetin` → `6,7,8-trimethoxy…`
(methylating a hydroxy *gives* a methoxy, so they agree chemically).

So the local version finds the known case and nothing new. Either the
wrong-compound class is genuinely rare, or it needs (a) to be found. I would not
deploy (b) without the chemistry-aware refinement.

## Lead worth checking

The two flavones have **consecutive MFCD numbers** (…488 dihydroxy /
…489 dimethoxy). If that reflects an off-by-one in `compounds_to_cas.csv`,
neighbouring rows would be suspect too. Stated as a hypothesis — the CSV was not
read.

## Suggested action

Correct this record (the labelled compound has no ChEBI term, so §3 step 2 or 3
applies), and run detector (a) across the 256 `cas:`-primary records.

Related: #308, #320, #322.
title: 3',6-Dihydroxyflavone is mapped to a dimethoxy compound; internally self-consistent so no existing check catches it

body:
## Finding

`ingredient_type` is unset on **559 of 2,497** mapped records (22%), and the
distribution is not diffuse — it is one cohort:

| cohort | unset | total | |
|---|---|---|---|
| microbedecoder import | **511** | 520 | **98%** |
| everything else | 48 | 1,977 | 2% |

The 2026-08-04 microbedecoder import appears to write no `ingredient_type` at
all, and `AUTO_CLASSIFY_INGREDIENT_TYPE` never ran over that cohort. Records
from other paths carry it normally.

## Why it is load-bearing, not cosmetic

`ingredient_type` is what would let downstream logic distinguish three states
that currently look identical — an empty `chemical_properties` block:

- **empty because it is a mixture** — `Artificial_Sea_Salt`, a branded
  formulation with no structure to record;
- **empty because the term is a structure-free class** — `Ascorbate`, correctly
  on the bare-name anion class, where copying `L-ascorbate`'s structure in would
  be a *defect*;
- **empty and genuinely fillable** — `Ascomycin`, where CAS 104987-12-4 and a
  full structure are available from ChEBI.

Without it, any enrichment pass that treats "empty" as "needs filling" will
corrupt the middle group while fixing the third. That is the root confusion
behind #316, and it makes this a prerequisite for widening enrichment rather
than an independent cleanup.

A second symptom: the few microbedecoder records that *do* carry a value can
carry a stale one. `Catalase` has `ingredient_type: SINGLE_INGREDIENT` with the
recorded reason "(CHEBI primary)" — but it has had no CHEBI primary since the
June 2026 repair moved it to NCIT.

## Suggested action

Run `AUTO_CLASSIFY_INGREDIENT_TYPE` over the microbedecoder cohort, and add the
classifier to the import path so the next ingest does not reproduce the gap.

Note the classifier has its own coverage hole worth fixing at the same time: it
recognises `infusion` as a complex-material pattern but has no `serum` rule,
which is why `Brain_Heart_Infusion` is classified `UNDEFINED_MIXTURE` while its
sibling `Bovine_Calf_Serum` is unset. Worth sweeping
serum/plasma/extract/digest/hydrolysate.

Query that sizes it: records with a `CREATED_AS_UNMAPPED` event dated
2026-08-04 and no `ingredient_type`.

Related: #316, #322.
title: ingredient_type is unset on 98% of the microbedecoder cohort (511/520)

body:
## The guard

A ChEBI term with **no structural annotation at all** (no InChIKey, SMILES or
formula) is a role class, a grouping class or a family class — not an individual
substance. Proposed check: *reject a candidate term with no structure when the
ingredient is expected to be a substance.*

**Result: 145 records are mapped to such a term, 117 of them `EXACT_MATCH`.**

```
EXACT_MATCH    117
NARROW_MATCH    23
SYNONYM_MATCH    2
LEXICAL_MATCH    2
BROAD_MATCH      1
```

It needs no domain knowledge and catches defects already confirmed separately —
`Bicine` (CHEBI:39065, grouping class), `Bisabolene` (CHEBI:49235, family class
over 16 terms), `Aluminium sulfate` (CHEBI:74772) — and would have blocked the
`Vibriostat` near-miss, where ChEBI has *both* the compound (CHEBI:73908) and a
role class (CHEBI:73911) and the string `vibriostatic agent` is simultaneously
the role class's label and a synonym of the compound.

## Not all 145 are defects

Many are correct: `Agar`, `Polysaccharides`, `arabinogalactan`, `amylopectin`
are genuinely polymers or classes with no single structure, and a class label
mapped to a class term is right. The grade is the problem — `EXACT_MATCH` to a
class asserts the ingredient **is** that class.

## The clearest subset: 10 records mapped to a bare compositional class

| term | records |
|---|---|
| `CHEBI:26714 sodium salt` | 8 — `D-Glucose-6-Phosphate sodium salt`, `TAPS sodium salt`, `Sulfamethazine sodium salt`, `3'-sialyllactose sodium salt`, `6'-O-sialyllactose sodium salt`, `2-oxobutyric acid sodium salt`, `DL-3-Hydroxyisobutyric acid sodium salt`, `Sulfaquinoxaline sodium salt` |
| `CHEBI:26218 potassium salt` | 2 — `5-Keto-D-Gluconic Acid potassium salt`, `D-Saccharic acid potassium salt` |

`D-Glucose-6-Phosphate sodium salt` → `sodium salt` retains the *counterion* and
discards the compound. All ten are graded `NARROW_MATCH`, which is at least
honest, but the mapping carries almost no information: eight unrelated
ingredients all resolve to the same node.

These are strong candidates for a `kgmicrobe.compound:` registry term instead —
"no ontology term denotes this" is more useful than "it is a sodium salt".

## Suggested action

1. Add the structure check as a **candidate filter** at mapping time — it is the
   cheapest of the guards proposed so far and needs no chemistry lookup.
2. Re-grade the 117 `EXACT_MATCH`-to-a-class records (overlaps #317).
3. Re-ground the 10 bare-compositional-class records.

Related: #316, #317, #319, #320, #321.
title: 145 records map to structureless CHEBI class terms; 117 graded EXACT_MATCH

body:
## The check

Flag any record whose `preferred_term` names a hydrate (`x n H2O`, `·nH2O`,
`hydrate`) while its recorded formula/SMILES/InChI contain **no water
component**. Purely mechanical.

**Result: 26 records.**

## Why the existing CAS-vs-structure check cannot see this

Both compared fields are populated from the same ChEBI term by
`AUTO_BACKFILL_CHEBI_CHEMISTRY`, so they agree **by construction**. The check
compares the record against itself; the *label* is the only field carrying the
contradicting information, and nothing was comparing against it.

## The sharper pattern: one term absorbing many distinct hydrates

**10 ontology terms carry 26 distinct hydrate labels between them:**

| term | absorbs |
|---|---|
| CHEBI:34683 | `Na2HPO4 x 2/3/6/7/12 H2O` — **five** different hydrates |
| CHEBI:35696 | `CoCl2 x 2/4/6 H2O` |
| CHEBI:34887 | `NiCl2 x 2/5/6 H2O` |
| CHEBI:75832 | `FeSO4 x 5/6/7 H2O` |
| CHEBI:23414 | `CuSO4 x 2/4 H2O` |
| CHEBI:30812 | `FeCl2 x 6/7 H2O` |
| CHEBI:86360 | `MnSO4 x 1/7 H2O` |
| CHEBI:53001 | `NiSO4 x 6/7 H2O` |

Different hydrates are different substances with different formula weights and
different CAS numbers. Collapsed onto one term they are indistinguishable
downstream — a recipe calling for the heptahydrate and one calling for the
dihydrate become the same node.

**The assignment is demonstrably arbitrary.** Magnesium sulfate splits across two
terms *by notation rather than by chemistry*:

```
CHEBI:32599  <- "MgSO4 x 6 H2O",  "MgSO4·7H2O"
CHEBI:31795  <- "MgSO4 x 7 H2O",  "MgSO4·H2O"
```

The **same** hydration number (7) lands on two different terms depending on
whether the label was written `x 7 H2O` or `·7H2O`. That is lexical matching
with no chemistry behind it.

One record states the contradiction outright: `Na2-EDTA x 2 H2O` carries
`ontology_label: EDTA disodium salt (anhydrous)`.

## Triage forks three ways — do not mass-apply

Established from three worked cases:

1. **The label is wrong.** `CaSO4 x 7 H2O` — no calcium sulfate heptahydrate
   exists (ChEBI has anhydrous/hemi/dihydrate only). Probably a `2`→`7` slip,
   but confirming needs the source recipes read. MediaDive maps
   `CaSO4 x 2 H2O` correctly, so it does distinguish these when they are real.
2. **The label is right and the ontology is deficient.** `CeCl3 x 7 H2O` is the
   standard commercial form; ChEBI has **no** cerium chloride hydrate at all.
   Ignoring the waters here is a **51% formula-weight error** (246 → 373).
   Candidate for a registry term.
3. **Neither side is definite.** `Cefsulodin sodium salt hydrate` — no hydrate
   term in any ontology *and* the label states no hydration number. Nothing to
   encode; the fix is dropping `EXACT_MATCH` and recording why.

So a lexical `x n H2O` sweep would fix (1) and corrupt (2).

## Suggested action

Add the detector as a standing check, then triage the 26 by the fork above.
The `Na2HPO4` five-way and `CoCl2`/`NiCl2` three-way collapses are the highest
value — they are the cases where distinct media ingredients have become
indistinguishable.

## Provenance

Detector proposed by the Claude research lane after the CAS-vs-structure check
passed on three defective records in one batch, with the correct diagnosis of
why it structurally could not catch them. Verified repo-wide.
Related: #315, #317, #320.
title: 26 hydrate-named records map to anhydrous terms; 10 terms absorb multiple distinct hydrates

body:
## The check

For every record carrying both a `cas_rn` and a CHEBI `ontology_id`, ask which
CHEBI term ChEBI itself registers that CAS against:

```
CAS -> CHEBI index from chebi.db (oio:hasDbXref, 29,736 CAS numbers)

records with CAS + CHEBI id        1370
  CAS registered on THIS term      1074
  CAS not in ChEBI at all           206
  CAS registered on a DIFFERENT term  90   <- defect candidates
```

**This class is invisible to InChIKey comparison**, which is why it survived the
CAS-vs-structure checking done so far: the mis-mapped term is usually a
parent/grouping class with no structure at all, so there is no key to compare.
The failure mode is a name lookup landing on a parent while the CAS points at
the specific child.

## Cross-validation

The check independently rediscovers four defects found separately, one at a time,
by the research lane — before this query existed:

| record | CURIE | CAS points to |
|---|---|---|
| `Ca-pantothenate` | CHEBI:29032 `(R)-pantothenate` | **CHEBI:31345 Calcium pantothenate** (the #315 merge) |
| `02_Thiamine_Pyrophosphate` | CHEBI:9532 | CHEBI:18290 `…diphosphate chloride` |
| `Bicine` | CHEBI:39065 (structureless class) | CHEBI:40957 `N,N-bis(2-hydroxyethyl)glycine` |
| `Aluminium sulfate` | CHEBI:74772 (class) | CHEBI:74768 `aluminium sulfate (anhydrous)` |
| `Bisabolene` | CHEBI:49235 (family class) | CHEBI:49240 `alpha-bisabolene` |

Four separate agents reaching five of these independently, and a mechanical query
reproducing all of them, is good evidence the remaining 85 are real.

## Two sub-classes, different remedies — do not mass-apply

**(a) CURIE is a parent; the label names the specific child.** Fix the CURIE.
`Bicine` (a structureless grouping class with a disjunctive definition),
`Bisabolene` (family over 16 terms — note `C15H24` is shared by all of them, so
a formula check passes on the wrong term), `Ca-pantothenate`, `Aluminium sulfate`,
`alpha-Lactose` → `Alpha-lactose monohydrate`, `Carboxymethyl cellulose` →
`carboxymethylcellulose sodium`.

**(b) CURIE is correctly generic for a generic label; the *CAS* is over-specific.**
Fix or drop the CAS, not the mapping. `Arginine` (CHEBI:29016, stereo-agnostic —
correct for a bare label) whose CAS 74-79-3 is L-arginine's; `Ascorbic acid`
(CHEBI:22652) with L-ascorbic acid's CAS; `D-Ribose` with D-ribofuranose's.

Sub-class (b) is the same shape as the bare-anion convention in #319: a
deliberately generic term is right for a generic label, and it is the
*over-specific companion field* that is wrong. Getting this backwards would
break correct records.

## Suggested action

Triage the 90 into (a) and (b); the discriminator is whether the record's own
label is generic or specific. Then add the query as a standing check — it is
cheap, needs only `chebi.db`, and catches a class nothing else does.

Also worth noting the 206 "CAS not in ChEBI at all": not a defect by itself, but
it is the population where a wrong CAS can hide indefinitely, since neither this
check nor an InChIKey comparison can adjudicate it.

## Provenance

Proposed by the Claude research lane after it hit the same shape three times
(`Bicine`, `Bisabolene`, `02_Thiamine_Pyrophosphate`) and observed that InChIKey
comparison structurally cannot catch it. Verified repo-wide against chebi.db.
Related: #315, #316, #317, #319.
title: 90 records whose CAS-RN is registered in ChEBI against a different term than their CURIE

body:
## Finding

MIM applies a real, load-bearing convention when grounding bare anion labels:

> Ground a bare anion label (`Fumarate`, `Citrate`, `Lactate`) to the
> fully-deprotonated CHEBI class **where one exists**; otherwise to the
> bare-name class.

**It is written down nowhere.** A search across all `*.md` and `*.yaml` outside
`data/` for `bare anion` / `bare-name` / `fully deprotonated` returns one
unrelated hit in a 2026 batch-suggestions note. The convention exists only in
per-record `evidence.notes` on the records that already applied it, and in issue
#213 discussion.

A curator working the residual reconstructed it by reading 12 sibling records
and generalising — correctly, as it happens, but that is inference from
observed practice, not a documented rule. The next one may generalise it wrong.

## Why it matters more than a typical doc gap

The rule has a **per-record branch that is easy to miss**, and both sides of it
are currently live in the data:

- `Aspartate` → should be `CHEBI:29995 aspartate(2-)`; it is currently on
  `CHEBI:132943 aspartate`, a structure-free, definition-free class. The
  structural analogue `Glutamate` is already on `CHEBI:29987 glutamate(2-)`, so
  the data is internally inconsistent. 431 occurrences — the highest-traffic
  record found in the lane so far.
- `Ascorbate` → the bare-name class **is** correct here, because no
  `ascorbate(1-)`/`(2-)` term exists in ChEBI (verified: `CHEBI:22651`'s only
  child is `L-ascorbate`). Rewriting it to an `X(n-)` term would be wrong.

So a mass-application of "always use the deprotonated form" would fix Aspartate
and break Ascorbate, Succinate and Malate. The "where one exists" clause is the
whole rule, and it is exactly the part an undocumented convention loses.

A second consequence: `ols-label-exact-chebi` ranks **primary labels only**,
which is why `Aspartate` landed on the class in the first place — the matcher
cannot implement a convention nobody wrote down.

## Suggested action

Document it in `MAPPING_SEMANTICS.md` alongside the predicate semantics, with:

- the rule and its `where one exists` branch,
- how to test the branch (search ChEBI for `<label>(n-)`; check the bare-name
  class for structure/definition — a structure-free class is a signal, not a
  target),
- the worked examples on both sides (Aspartate vs Ascorbate),
- and the note that structure-free classes must **not** be chemistry-enriched
  (an enrichment pass copying `L-ascorbate`'s structure onto the `ascorbate`
  class would be a #316-style defect).

Related: #213, #312, #315, #316, #317.
title: The bare-anion grounding convention is undocumented; curators are inferring it from practice

body:
Two defects in ChEBI itself, both verified, both with concrete consequences for
MIM curation. Filing here to track our side; they should also go upstream.

---

## 1. `ss` → `ß` → `beta` label corruption — 194 terms

ChEBI labels for a range of natural products have had `ss` transliterated to `ß`
and then expanded to the literal string `beta`, welding it inside the word:

| terms | corrupted label | correct name |
|---|---|---|
| 38 | `Thalabetaospiramide A` | Thalassospiramide A |
| 35 | `Abybetaomicin D` | Abyssomicin D |
| 28 | `Brabetaicicene E` | Brassicicene E |
| 21 | `Preubetaomerin EG2` | Preussomerin EG2 |
| 18 | `Colobetaolactone VI` | Colossolactone VI |
| 12 | `Rubetaujaponol H` | Russujaponol H |
| 10 | `Preubetain B` | Preussin B |
| 8 each | `Mabetaetolide`, `Sargabetaopenilline`, `Minutibetaamide`, `Ganocolobetausin` | Massetolide, Sargassopenilline, Minutissamide, Ganocolossusin |

Every one restores exactly under `label.replace("beta", "ss")`.

**Counting caveat.** A naive `[a-z]beta[a-z]` scan returns 403 labels, but that
over-counts: `chlorbetamide`, `ulobetasol`, `tembetarine` and
`gamma-butyrobetaine` are legitimate names containing `beta`. 194 is the count
restricted to stems that restore to a documented natural-product family, so it
is a floor, not the full extent.

**Consequence for MIM.** No MIM record is currently *mapped* to a corrupted term
(checked: 0). The damage is that label-based matching cannot find them, silently.
Demonstrated: `Abyssomicin_D` sits on `mesh:C512805` — valid and label-exact, but
carrying **no structure, formula or CAS** — while the structurally-defined
`CHEBI:197743` went uncited because its label reads `Abybetaomicin D`. The
record's original OLS search returning LOW confidence was this bug, not a
genuinely absent term.

This will keep recurring for any natural product with `ss` in its name.

---

## 2. `CHEBI:156543 ammonium persulfate` — structure contradicts its own definition

ChEBI's annotations for this 3-star term describe a **different compound** from
the one it defines:

| field | ChEBI value | implies |
|---|---|---|
| definition | "…two of the terminal hydroxy groups of **peroxydisulfuric acid** are deprotonated…" | persulfate, S(VI), **O8**S2 |
| `generalized_empirical_formula` | `2H4N.O6S2` | peroxydisul**fite**, S(IV), O6 |
| `smiles_string` | `O=S([O-])OOS(=O)[O-].[NH4+].[NH4+]` | S(IV) |
| `mass` | 196.206 | (persulfate is 228.20) |

So the formula, SMILES, InChI, InChIKey and mass are internally consistent with
each other but contradict the term's definition, its own
`has part → CHEBI:29267 peroxydisulfate (O8S2)` axiom, and its CAS.

**Consequence for MIM.** `AUTO_BACKFILL_CHEBI_CHEMISTRY` copied the wrong
formula, InChI and mass onto our `Ammonium_Persulfate` record. The CURIE is
right; the chemistry is wrong, and it came from trusting ChEBI's annotations.

---

## Suggested actions

1. Report both upstream to ChEBI.
2. Correct the `Ammonium_Persulfate` chemistry locally and mark the source as
   contradicted, rather than waiting on the upstream fix.
3. Re-run grounding for `Abyssomicin_D` against `CHEBI:197743`, which is a
   better target than the structureless MeSH term — noting the promotion should
   record that the ChEBI *label* is corrupt so a future label-correspondence
   check does not "fix" our record to match it (cf. #299, and the
   `id-label-correspondence` gate).
4. Consider a general guard: an ontology annotation that contradicts its own
   term definition should not be silently backfilled. This is the same trust
   failure as #315/#317 — enrichment and grading believing a source without
   checking it.

Found by the Claude research lane on `Ammonium_Persulfate` and `Abyssomicin_D`;
both verified independently against OLS4 and the local chebi.db.
Related: #309, #315, #316, #317.
title: Upstream ChEBI defects blocking MIM curation: corrupted labels (194 terms) and a wrong ammonium persulfate structure

body:
## Finding

Of **1,864** records graded `EXACT_MATCH`, **356** carry a CHEBI term whose
primary label equals neither the record's `preferred_term` nor any recorded
synonym. Resolving each against the local `chebi.db` synonym lists splits them
cleanly:

| | count | |
|---|---|---|
| justified by a ChEBI **synonym** | **297** | term is right, **grade is wrong** |
| matched by **nothing** in ChEBI (label or synonym) | **59** | needs individual review |

## The 297 are mis-graded by the schema's own definition

`mediaingredientmech.yaml` is unambiguous:

```yaml
EXACT_MATCH:    Direct exact match to ontology term
SYNONYM_MATCH:  Matches known synonym in ontology
```

A label matching a ChEBI *synonym* rather than the primary label is
`SYNONYM_MATCH` by definition. This is not a judgement call — it is 16% of all
`EXACT_MATCH` records disagreeing with the enum they use.

The grade is load-bearing: it is what tells a downstream consumer how much to
trust an identity assertion, and `EXACT_MATCH` is the strongest claim available.

## The 59 need review, and are not one thing

Sub-classes visible on inspection:

- **Genuine scope loss** — the label carries a qualifier the term does not:
  `b-Glucan from Oat` → `beta-D-glucan` (source lost),
  `amylopectin from maize` → `amylopectin`,
  `Acetate (carbon source)` → `acetate`,
  `Ammonium chloride (nitrogen source)` → `ammonium chloride`,
  `Alpha-Toxicarol (Dl)` → `Toxicarol` (racemate → unspecified).
- **A semantic error** — `Aromatic hydrocarbon` → `polycyclic arene`. Not a
  synonym relation in either direction: benzene is an aromatic hydrocarbon and
  is not polycyclic. The term is narrower than the label.
- **Trivial-vs-systematic naming**, arguably fine but not *exact*:
  `Butanol` → `butan-1-ol`, `2-Ethylhexanol` → `2-ethylhexan-1-ol`,
  `2-Piperidinone` → `piperidin-2-one`.
- **Formula-as-label**: `KNO2` → `potassium nitrite`, `NH42CO3` →
  `ammonium carbonate`. The formula is not a ChEBI string at all.
- **Misspellings that nonetheless resolved correctly**:
  `Pyromelitic acid` → `pyromellitic acid`, `Thioglycollic acid` →
  `thioglycolic acid`. Compound is right; `EXACT_MATCH` is not.

## Reproduction

```python
# for each EXACT_MATCH record with a CHEBI ontology_id:
#   skip if preferred_term or a recorded synonym == ontology_label (normalised)
#   else look up the term's synonyms in ~/.data/oaklib/chebi.db:
#     any match -> should be SYNONYM_MATCH   (297)
#     no match  -> review                     (59)
```

Normalisation is case- and punctuation-insensitive, so this does not flag mere
capitalisation differences.

## Suggested action

The 297 are a safe mechanical re-grade to `SYNONYM_MATCH` with a
`curation_history` entry — no ontology_id changes, no SSSOM object changes.
Note the SSSOM predicate may need review alongside it, since `skos:exactMatch`
rows resting on a synonym match are the same overstatement.

The 59 need per-record calls; the scope-loss and `Aromatic hydrocarbon` cases
are real defects, the naming-convention ones probably just want re-grading too.

## Provenance

Surfaced by the Claude research lane, which flagged `EXACT_MATCH` as
unsupportable on `1-naphtylacetic_Acid`, `5-Hydroxyoctanoate`, `Angustmycin` and
`Aluminium_Sulfate` independently, then generalised repo-wide against chebi.db.
Related: #309, #312, #315, #316.
title: 297 records graded EXACT_MATCH are synonym matches; 59 more match nothing in ChEBI

body:
## Finding

`AUTO_BACKFILL_CHEBI_CHEMISTRY` resolves chemistry from ChEBI annotations, so a
record whose primary identifier is not a CHEBI (or CAS) CURIE is structurally
invisible to it — not "not yet enriched", but *can never be*.

Coverage of `chemical_properties` by identifier namespace:

| prefix | records | no chem props | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `chebi` | 1826 | 494 | 27% |
| `cas` | 256 | 3 | 1% |
| `mesh` | 68 | 67 | **99%** |
| `ncit` | 44 | 44 | **100%** |
| `micro` | 45 | 43 | 96% |
| `kgmicrobe.ingredient` | 123 | 121 | 98% |
| `kgmicrobe.compound` | 90 | 87 | 97% |
| `foodon` | 30 | 25 | 83% |

## Scope — the honest number is 112, not 387

Most of the non-CHEBI namespaces hold **materials, not compounds**. A FOODON
food, a MICRO taxon, or a `kgmicrobe.ingredient` extract has no molecular
formula, and an empty `chemical_properties` is correct for those.

The gap that matters is **MeSH (68) + NCIT (44) = 112 records that name
individual chemicals** yet are excluded by construction. Example:
`Amphotericin_A` (`mesh:C041989`) — a well-characterised compound,
C47H75NO17 / CAS 1405-32-9, verified against PubChem — with
`chemical_properties: None recorded` and no path to ever gaining any.

## Secondary defect

Records in this set carry curation notes like *"Pending curator promotion to a
CHEBI/NCIT primary identifier"* that are **stale**: for `Amphotericin_A` no such
term exists (ChEBI has amphotericin B and its methyl ester, not A — checked by
label and synonym query). The note implies a pending action that cannot be taken.

## Suggested fix

Enrich from a structure source keyed on something other than the CHEBI CURIE.
PubChem resolves cleanly by name, by CAS-RN, and by MeSH concept, and is already
a dependency of `chemical_properties_client.py`. A CAS-first lookup would cover
most of the 112, since these records generally have or can get a CAS-RN.

Worth pairing with #315 — enrichment writing structure fields onto records whose
label denotes a *different* salt/protonation state is how that defect class
arose, so any widened enrichment should check the salt/charge form it is
importing rather than trusting the name match.

## Provenance

Surfaced by the Claude research lane on `Amphotericin_A`, then quantified
repo-wide. Related: #309, #312, #315.
title: Chemical-property enrichment is CHEBI-only, so 112 MeSH/NCIT chemical records can never be enriched

body:
## Finding

Ten records whose **label explicitly names a counterion or says "salt"** carry a
mapping whose **recorded structure is a net-charged ion**. Seven are graded
`EXACT_MATCH` — the strongest identity claim available, asserting that a salt
*is* its anion.

| net charge | identifier | quality | label | term (verified OLS4) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| −2 | CHEBI:16810 | **EXACT_MATCH** | `Na2 alpha-ketoglutarate` | `2-oxoglutarate(2-)` |
| −2 | CHEBI:29988 | **EXACT_MATCH** | `Na-glutamate` | `L-glutamate(2-)` |
| −2 | CHEBI:30924 | **EXACT_MATCH** | `Na-tartrate` | `L-tartrate(2-)` |
| −1 | CHEBI:29032 | **EXACT_MATCH** | `Ca-pantothenate` | `(R)-pantothenate` |
| −1 | CHEBI:35899 | **EXACT_MATCH** | `Na-crotonate` | `crotonate` |
| +1 | CHEBI:46020 | **EXACT_MATCH** | `Tetramethyl ammonium` | (cation) |
| −2 | cas:12208-13-8 | FALLBACK_REGISTRY | `potassium hexahydroxoantimonate` | — |
| −1 | cas:207511-06-6 | NARROW_MATCH | `L-Malic acid disodium salt monohydrate` | — |
| +1 | cas:9067-32-7 | NARROW_MATCH | `Hyaluronic acid sodium salt from S. equi` | — |
| +1 | kgmicrobe.compound:… | CLOSE_MATCH | `Tetramethyl ammonium chloride` | — |

All five CHEBI labels above verified live against OLS4; none obsolete.

## Why these are not covered by the #213 convention

MIM deliberately grounds **bare anion labels** (`Fumarate`, `Citrate`, `Lactate`)
to the fully-deprotonated CHEBI class, and that is correct — a bare label carries
no counterion, and the anion is the species present at growth-medium pH.

These ten are a different case: the label **names the counterion**
(`Na2 …`, `Ca-…`, `… sodium salt`). Sodium glutamate and glutamate(2−) are
different substances with different formulas, masses and CAS numbers. So the
convention does not license `EXACT_MATCH` here, and the anion mapping — while a
reasonable *close/narrow* relation — overstates as identity.

Note also `Na-glutamate`: monosodium glutamate is the **mono**-anion salt, so
even the charge state of the current target is off by one.

## Detection

Mechanical and high-precision. Net charge must be computed across **both** InChI
layers — `/q` alone gives 119 false positives, because a neutral salt like AlCl3
is written `/q+3;;;/p-3`:

```python
net = sum(component /q charges) + /p          # non-zero  => recorded structure is an ion
defect = net != 0 and label names a counterion or "salt"
```

That narrows 119 → 40 → **10**, with no false positives in the 10 on inspection.

## Suggested action

Per record: either re-ground to a CHEBI salt term where one exists, or keep the
anion term and downgrade `mapping_quality` to `CLOSE_MATCH`/`NARROW_MATCH` with
the reason recorded. The `EXACT_MATCH` grade is the part that is indefensible.

Worth adding the check to the validation suite so a future promotion sweep
cannot reintroduce it.

## Provenance

Surfaced by the Claude research lane on `1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium_Lysine`
(CHEBI:61326 is the [C2mim]⁺ cation alone; the ingredient is a neutral salt),
then generalised repo-wide. Related: #312 (ledger triage), #309 (the two-lane
harness).
title: Salt-named records mapped EXACT_MATCH to the bare anion (10 records)

body:
Follow-up to #308. PR #309 corrected 6 of the 10 affected records; these four
plus one synonym were deliberately left because each needs a judgement call
rather than a mechanical fix.

## Four records with truncated locants

| slug | current | the problem |
|---|---|---|
| `2-dimethylsuccinic_Acid` | CHEBI:167506 `2,3-dimethylsuccinic acid`, CLOSE_MATCH | `2,2-` and `2,3-dimethylsuccinic acid` are both real. Split-keep-last from `2,3-` yields `3-`, not `2-`, so `2,2-` is the more likely original — but "more likely" is not evidence. |
| `2-tetrachloroethane` | UNMAPPED_0785 | Probably `1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane`, unverified. |
| `4-Diamino-6` | UNMAPPED_0620 | Trailing `-6` suggests a longer name (`2,4-diamino-6-...`). Too little survives. |
| `4-diol` | UNMAPPED_0791 | Only the suffix survives. |

For the last three, the upstream source row is the only way to recover the
original string — which is another reason to fix the ingest (#308) rather than
guess here.

## One synonym in the wrong record

`5-didehydro-D-gluconate` was absorbed as a RAW_TEXT synonym into
`5-dehydro-D-gluconate.yaml` (CHEBI:58143) on the rationale that "'didehydro' is
a typo for 'dehydro'; same compound". That rationale is the same error #308
corrected on the acid: verified against OLS4,

- CHEBI:58143 = `5-dehydro-D-gluconate`
- CHEBI:11449 = `2,5-didehydro-D-gluconate`

are distinct. The synonym should be removed from CHEBI:58143 and re-homed to a
record for CHEBI:11449 (no record currently claims it). Not done in #309 because
removing it without creating the new record would drop the source label entirely,
and creating a record is more than a correction.

## Standing check

`scripts/check_truncated_locants.py` currently reports exactly these four and
exits non-zero when any are found. Worth wiring into CI once they are resolved,
per #308 — note the non-zero exit will fail the build until then.
title: Finish the comma-truncation cleanup: 4 curator calls + the CHEBI:11449 synonym re-homing

body:
## Finding

`scripts/validate_records_against_research.py` (#309) compares each ingredient
record against the deep-research report for that same ingredient. Over the 527
records researched so far it found **71 `STATUS_CONFLICT`s** — the record asserts
an ontology mapping while its own report recommended `UNMAPPED`.

**Every one of them was written by the same mechanical sweep,
`promote_resolved_unmapped`.** That is the #203/#263 pattern recurring: a
plausible identifier promoted by a mechanism that never decided anything.

## Important caveat — do not treat all 71 as defects

The Edison/PaperQA3 lane cannot open an ontology page. Its reports say so
verbatim ("no ChEBI CURIE was verified in the retrieved evidence"), so it
defaults to "retain UNMAPPED" whenever it cannot confirm a term — which is most
of the time. An Edison "retain UNMAPPED" on its own is therefore weak evidence.

That is exactly why the second (Claude) lane exists, and it already resolved 22
of these: `LANE_DISAGREEMENT_RESOLVED` marks a conflict the Claude lane cleared
by resolving the term Edison could not. Those 22 need no action.

## Triage order

Work `mappings/record_research_validation.md`, most severe first:

1. **17 `BOTH_LANES_DISPUTE`** — both independent lanes dispute the mapping.
   Strongest signal in the ledger; start here.
2. **`P1 CURIE_REFUTED`** — a report names the record's exact CURIE and argues
   against it. The quoted line usually names the right term.
3. **`P1 VERDICT_REFUTES`** — a per-field verdict table refutes an identity
   field and supplies a corrected value.
4. The remainder of the `STATUS_CONFLICT`s, checking `promoted_by` and
   `documented_rationale`.

Each row carries the quoted report line that produced it, so most are a one-read
decision: keep with a written justification, downgrade `mapping_quality`, or
demote.

## Note on coverage

The ledger currently covers 527 of 2,841 records; the Edison sweep is ongoing
(~30 records/hour, account-capped). Re-run the validator as it completes — these
counts will grow.
title: Triage the 71 records asserting a mapping their own research report advised against

body:
## Finding

`tests/test_check_chebi_currency.py::test_kgmicrobe_default_is_a_sibling_not_a_hardcoded_home`
fails on this machine and passes in `/tmp`. The branch under test changes nothing
in that area — the failure is environment-dependent.

## Cause

The test detects a hardcoded home directory by string-matching `/Users/`:

```python
assert "/Users/" not in str(mod.default_kgm_chebi())
```

The default is now correctly computed as a *sibling of the repo*, which is the
behaviour the test was written to enforce. But when the repo itself lives under
`/Users/...` — i.e. every macOS checkout — the correctly-computed sibling path
also contains `/Users/`, and the assertion fires:

```
AssertionError: assert '/Users/' not in
  '/Users/marcin/.../KG-Microbe/kg-microbe/data/raw/chebi.owl.gz'
```

So the test passes only where the repo is outside `/Users` (CI, `/tmp`), and
fails for the developers it is meant to protect. It is asserting on the
*absolute path text* rather than on the property it cares about.

## Suggested fix

Assert the actual invariant — that the default is derived from the repo location
rather than pinned to one user — for example:

- the path is relative to the repo root's parent (`Path(...).parents[n]`), or
- it does not contain a *specific* username, or
- monkeypatch the repo root to a temp dir and assert the default moves with it.

The third is the real test: if the default tracks a relocated repo root, it
cannot be hardcoded.

Found during the adversarial review pass on #309. Pre-existing; not fixed there
because it is unrelated to that branch and the fix is a judgement call about
what the test should assert.
title: test_kgmicrobe_default_is_a_sibling_not_a_hardcoded_home fails for any checkout under /Users

body:
## Finding

Five records use zero-padded CAS Registry Numbers as their primary identifier:

```
cas:0124-09-4    (should be cas:124-09-4)
cas:0303-07-1    (should be cas:303-07-1)
cas:0305-01-1    (should be cas:305-01-1)
cas:0392-12-1    (should be cas:392-12-1)
cas:0612-05-5    (should be cas:612-05-5)
```

CAS Registry Numbers never carry leading zeros — the format is
`{2..7 digits}-{2 digits}-{1 check digit}`. The padding looks like alignment to a
fixed width somewhere in the ingest.

## Why it matters

These are *primary identifiers*, so the damage is not cosmetic:

- The CURIE does not resolve against CAS Common Chemistry or any CAS-aware
  resolver, so the identity anchor a `cas:`-primary record exists to provide
  does not actually anchor anything.
- Five rows in `mappings/ingredient_mappings.sssom.tsv` publish the padded form.
- Any downstream join on CAS-RN silently misses these five.

## Suggested fix

Normalise to the unpadded form across `data/curated/`, the generated
`data/ingredients/` view, and the SSSOM rows, with a `curation_history` entry
per record. Then add a check — a `cas:` local id matching `^0` is always wrong —
so a re-ingest cannot reintroduce it.

Note the identifier is the primary key, so this is an identifier change and
should go through the same collision guard `promote_resolved_unmapped.py` uses.

Found during the two-lane deep-research validation sweep (#309). Not fixed there
because it is a separate defect from the comma-truncation bug (#308) and touches
records that sweep did not otherwise change.
title: Five cas: identifiers carry leading zeros, making them non-resolvable

body:
## Summary

`data/custom/microbedecoder/unmapped_labels.tsv` and `ingredient_candidates.tsv`
contain **zero commas across 6,247 label rows**. That is not possible for
chemical nomenclature, where locants (`2,3-`, `3,4,5-`) are ubiquitous. Rows
sourced from `culturebotht` *do* retain commas, so this is specific to the
microbedecoder ingest path.

The mechanism appears to be **split on comma, keep the last field** — an
unquoted-CSV bug — rather than comma deletion:

| label as ingested | reconstructed original |
|---|---|
| `5-trimethoxybenzoate` | `3,4,5-trimethoxybenzoate` |
| `3-beta-d-glucan` | `1,3-beta-D-glucan` |
| `4-dihydroxy-biphenyl` | `3,4-` or `4,4'-dihydroxybiphenyl` |
| `5-didehydro-D-gluconic acid` | `2,5-didehydro-D-gluconic acid` |

## Why this is not cosmetic

A truncated name still *looks* like a valid chemical name, so matching grounds
it without complaint. Sometimes it lands on the right compound anyway. Sometimes
it lands on a different real compound:

- **`5-didehydro-D-gluconic_Acid`** is published in
  `mappings/ingredient_mappings.sssom.tsv:261` as `skos:exactMatch` to
  **CHEBI:17426 `5-dehydro-D-gluconic acid`** (C6H10O7, mono-keto).
  Verified against OLS4, the correct term is **CHEBI:18281
  `2,5-didehydro-D-gluconic acid`** (C6H8O7, di-keto). Different compounds.
  An `exactMatch` licenses node substitution in KG-Microbe.
- The same defect, unpublished: `5-didehydro-D-gluconate` was absorbed as a
  synonym into `5-dehydro-D-gluconate.yaml` (CHEBI:58143) on a "'didehydro' is
  a typo for 'dehydro'" rationale. It is CHEBI:11449 `2,5-didehydro-D-gluconate`.
- **`2-dimethylsuccinic_Acid`** is mapped `skos:closeMatch` to CHEBI:167506
  `2,3-dimethylsuccinic acid`. Under split-keep-last, `2,3-` would have yielded
  `3-`, not `2-`, so the original is more likely `2,2-dimethylsuccinic acid`
  (also a real compound). Needs a call.

## Standing check

`scripts/check_truncated_locants.py` (added in the branch below) encodes the
detectable signature: a multiplying prefix must carry as many locants as its
multiplier. It distinguishes substituent multipliers from alkane chain-length
stems, so `1-Pentanol` and `3-octanone` are correctly not flagged.

Current blast radius: **10 records**.

```
2-dichloroethane            CHEBI:27789   -> 1,2-dichloroethane
3-trichloropropane          CHEBI:34036   -> 1,2,3-Trichloropropane
2-6-dihydroxybenzoic_Acid   cas:0303-07-1
2-dimethylsuccinic_Acid     CHEBI:167506  -> 2,3-dimethylsuccinic acid
2-tetrachloroethane         UNMAPPED_0785
4-Diamino-6                 UNMAPPED_0620
4-dihydroxy-biphenyl        CHEBI:34367   -> biphenyl-4,4'-diol
4-diol                      UNMAPPED_0791
5-didehydro-D-gluconic_Acid CHEBI:17426   -> 5-dehydro-D-gluconic acid
5-trimethoxybenzoate        CHEBI:58989   -> 3,4,5-trimethoxybenzoate
```

## Suggested actions

1. Fix the upstream writer of `data/custom/microbedecoder/*.tsv` to quote fields
   or emit real TSV. Until then it will keep producing wrong mappings on refresh.
2. Retract the `skos:exactMatch` on line 261 and re-ground to CHEBI:18281.
3. Re-ground the `5-didehydro-D-gluconate` synonym absorption to CHEBI:11449.
4. Decide `2-dimethylsuccinic_Acid` (`2,2-` vs `2,3-`).
5. Wire `check_truncated_locants.py` into CI so refreshes cannot reintroduce this.

Found by the two-lane deep-research validation sweep (branch
`research/all-ingredient-deep-research`).
title: microbedecoder ingest strips commas from every chemical label, producing wrong mappings

body:
Found in the adversarial review of PR #305, which rescues this script from the closed PR #201 branch.

`scripts/promote_microbedecoder_residual.py` synthesises its SSSOM subject the same way #293 flags in `promote_resolved_unmapped.py`:

```python
slug = sanitize_filename(pref)
...
f"MIM:{slug}", pref, "skos:exactMatch", tid, label, ...
```

`export_individual_records.FilenameIndex` **never renames an existing per-record file** — deliberate, so paths stay stable. Recomputing the subject from `preferred_term` therefore disagrees with the on-disk stem whenever that stem predates the current naming rule:

```
file on disk:   data/ingredients/mapped/Na2glycerophosphate5h2o.yaml
SSSOM subject:  MIM:Na2glycerophosphate5H2O     <- recomputed, differs by case
```

`CurieNormalizer.resolve()` checks the subject against the known record set, so a recomputed subject that no file backs resolves to `UNKNOWN_SUBJECT` — which is exactly how #293 was discovered, after a bulk promotion.

## Why it needs its own issue rather than folding into #293

#293 is scoped to `promote_resolved_unmapped.py` and its fix is "use the existing file stem instead of recomputing". Same remedy here, but it is a **second, independent copy of the rule** — fixing #293 will not touch this file, and nothing links them. `sanitize_filename` is imported directly, so there is no shared helper to correct once.

Worth checking whether there is a third: grep for `sanitize_filename` across `scripts/` before fixing, and consider routing every SSSOM-subject derivation through one function that consults `FilenameIndex` rather than re-deriving.

## Severity

**Latent, not live.** The pass this script ran is complete and every row is a no-op today (its `STATUS` block records this, verified in #305: 20/20 SKIP on the PK-collision guard, 0 promotions). No bad subject is published from it right now.

It becomes live the moment someone re-points it with `--vetted` at a new manifest — which is a reuse path the script's own header advertises. PR #305 amends that header to warn about this issue and #306 rather than invite reuse, but the defect itself stays open.

Related: #293, #236, #305, #306, #201.
title: promote_microbedecoder_residual.py recomputes the SSSOM subject from preferred_term (#293 in a second script)

body:
Found while rescuing the script in PR #305, and deliberately left unfixed there — a rescue should land what actually ran.

`scripts/promote_microbedecoder_residual.py` resolves the OAK cache by hand:

```python
DB = {"CHEBI": Path.home() / ".data/oaklib/chebi.db",
      "NCIT":  Path.home() / ".data/oaklib/ncit.db"}
```

`Path.home() / ".data/oaklib"` is oaklib's *default*, not its actual location. oaklib resolves the cache through pystow, which honours `PYSTOW_HOME`. The repo already knows this — `scripts/check_chebi_currency.py` has:

```python
def oaklib_cache_dir() -> Path:
    """Resolved through pystow, which oaklib itself uses (oaklib/constants.py), so
    this honours PYSTOW_HOME. Deriving it from $HOME instead means a developer
    with PYSTOW_HOME set gets a check that reads — and a refresh that deletes —
    the wrong path, while reporting success."""
```

That docstring describes this defect exactly, and was written for a *read-only* check. Here the consequence is worse than a bad read.

## Why it matters more in this script

`canonical_label()` opens the db and raises `SystemExit` when a term has no `rdfs:label`:

```python
if not row:
    raise SystemExit(f"{cid} has no rdfs:label (absent / wrong id)")
```

For a developer with `PYSTOW_HOME` set, the connect either fails or opens a nonexistent/empty sqlite. The error the curator sees — *"CHEBI:NNNNN has no rdfs:label (absent / wrong id)"* — **blames the identifier for a path problem**. That is the same failure mode as #197: a tool stating a confident wrong conclusion about an id, which is what led someone to demote 17 valid terms.

It cannot silently corrupt data (the label lookup fails closed rather than writing a wrong label), so this is a usability/diagnosis defect, not a correctness one.

## Fix

Use the existing helper rather than adding a third copy of the rule:

```python
from check_chebi_currency import oaklib_cache_dir     # already sys.path-inserted: scripts/
CACHE = oaklib_cache_dir()
DB = {"CHEBI": CACHE / "chebi.db", "NCIT": CACHE / "ncit.db"}
```

The script already does `sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "scripts"))` for `export_individual_records`, so the import costs nothing new. Worth also checking `DB[pfx].is_file()` up front and saying *which path* was tried, so the failure names the real cause.

## Scope check before fixing

Grep for other hand-rolled `~/.data/oaklib` derivations — if there are more, this should be one sweep that routes them all through `oaklib_cache_dir()`, rather than three separate fixes.

Low priority: the script is a completed pass (its `STATUS` block says so) and every row is a no-op today. It matters if anyone re-points it with `--vetted` at a new manifest, which is the reuse path the same block advertises.

Related: #305, #201, #197.
title: promote_microbedecoder_residual.py hardcodes ~/.data/oaklib instead of resolving via pystow

body:
Found reviewing PR #302 (closes #210). Not a defect of that PR — it is the cost the fix knowingly pays, recorded so it is not rediscovered as a surprise.

## The ceiling now catches strictly less

`ID_OUT_OF_RANGE` fires when an id fails to resolve **and** its accession exceeds the ceiling. Raising `CHEBI` from 300000 to 1000000 was necessary (300000 sat below ChEBI's real 747618 range), but it means the verdict can now only fire on **8-digit** CHEBI accessions.

Every foreign identifier shorter than that reports `ID_NOT_FOUND` instead. `src/mediaingredientmech/curie.py:43-48` already names two real examples from this corpus:

> the PubChem CIDs that turned up wearing a CHEBI prefix include 6-digit values (503742, 867561) that sit *inside* the real range

`CHEBI:867561` is the bogus id from #170. Verified: it does not resolve in the local build, and at the new ceiling it reports `ID_NOT_FOUND`.

**Nothing is missed** — both verdicts are in `_ERROR_VERDICTS` and both are fatal. What is lost is the *diagnosis*: a curator sees "did not resolve" where they used to see "came from another registry", and for 6-and-7-digit CIDs they now get the less useful of the two.

## Why this is not simply "lower the ceiling back"

The two errors are asymmetric, and #193 measured which one is expensive:

- Ceiling too **low** → a real term is called foreign → a curator deletes a valid mapping. Cost: 17 demotions, two follow-up PRs, six records still being untangled a week later.
- Ceiling too **high** → a foreign id is called missing → a curator investigates and finds it is not real anyway. Cost: one OLS4 lookup.

So the current setting is the right side to err on. The point is that the ceiling was never the mechanism doing the work — **resolution** is. A digit-count heuristic cannot separate namespaces that overlap, and CHEBI and PubChem overlap across their whole shared range.

## What would actually discriminate

If the "is this from another registry?" question is worth answering at all, it wants evidence rather than arithmetic — e.g. on a non-resolving id, ask whether the accession resolves as a PubChem CID whose title matches the record's label. That is a positive identification, not an inference from width, and it works at 6 digits.

Alternatively: accept that `ID_OUT_OF_RANGE` is a narrow special case of `ID_NOT_FOUND`, document it as such, and stop implying the gate can tell the two apart in general. That is cheaper and may be the honest answer.

Either way the ceiling comment should say what the heuristic **cannot** do, which `curie.py` already does and `conf/id_label_targets.yaml` now partly does.

Related: #210, #303, #197, #170, #193.
title: After #210 the accession ceiling can only fire on 8+ digit ids — weaker than its verdict name claims

body:
Found reviewing PR #302 (closes #210). #210 task 3 asked to soften the `ID_OUT_OF_RANGE` wording "so it states the evidence rather than the conclusion". PR #302 did that for every surface it could reach; this is the part it deliberately could not.

## What is left

`scripts/validate_id_label_correspondence.py` still asserts the conclusion in four places:

| line | text |
|---|---|
| 142 | `a foreign identifier (typically a PubChem CID) wearing an OBO prefix.` |
| 520 | `always a foreign identifier wearing an OBO prefix (PubChem CIDs reach` |
| 766 | `ceiling is a foreign identifier wearing an OBO prefix (PubChem CIDs run to` |
| 889 | `ID_OUT_OF_RANGE explicitly signals a foreign identifier` |

These are comments, so a curator does not read them directly — but they are what the next person editing the gate reasons from, and they are the source the curator-facing docs were paraphrasing.

The verdict itself also carries **no `detail`**: `classify()` returns bare `{**base, "verdict": "ID_OUT_OF_RANGE"}` (line 526), while every other judgement-call verdict in the file carries a `detail` string explaining itself. So the only thing a curator sees in `reports/label_drift.tsv` is the verdict *name*, and the name is the conclusion.

## Why PR #302 did not do it

That file is vendored **byte-identical** from CultureMech — confirmed, not assumed:

```
312ee4af1351c54bcce065829ac0083b  CultureMech/scripts/validate_id_label_correspondence.py
312ee4af1351c54bcce065829ac0083b  MediaIngredientMech/scripts/validate_id_label_correspondence.py
```

(`conf/id_label_targets.yaml` is *not* shared — different hashes — which is why the ceiling itself could be fixed here.) #210's own closing note says script changes go through `CultureBotAI/CultureMech` first, so editing it here would fork the vendored copy to fix a comment.

## Proposed change, to land in CultureMech then vendor back

1. Reword the four comments to state the evidence: *"did not resolve here, and the accession is beyond anything this ontology has minted — most likely an identifier from another registry."*
2. Add a `detail` to the verdict, e.g. `f"did not resolve; accession {local} is above the configured {prefix} ceiling {max_accession}"`. That puts the ceiling that fired into the report, which is what would have made #193's mistake visible at a glance.
3. Note in the comment that the ceiling is a **weak** heuristic (see #304) and must never be the sole reason to reject an id an ontology can confirm — the phrasing `src/mediaingredientmech/curie.py:43-48` already uses.

Blocked on: CultureBotAI/CultureMech#247, which should carry the same edit.

Related: #210, #197, #193.
title: ID_OUT_OF_RANGE still states its conclusion, in the one file MIM must not edit

body:
Minor, found in the review of the #299 revert.

`mappings/ingredient_mappings.sssom.tsv` header:

    # mapping_set_version: "2026-08-06"
    # mapping_date: "2026-08-06"

The mapping set has changed twice since that date on
`curation/edison-unmapped-sweep` — `d745c424` added 5 promotions on 2026-08-07,
`87bd0aad` rewrote 70 subject rows the same day — and neither bumped the header.
Checked `d745c424`: it touched no `# mapping_` line.

The writers (`promote_resolved_unmapped`, `promote_microbedecoder_reviewed`,
`reground_mapped_record`, `relabel_mapped_record`, `merge_mapped_records`,
`anchor_cas_hydrate_records`) all append or rewrite rows without touching the
header, so the version only moves when someone edits it by hand. It is
consequently wrong most of the time.

SSSOM consumers use `mapping_set_version` to decide whether they hold the
current set. A version that does not move is worse than absent — it reads as
"unchanged since 2026-08-06" to anything caching on it.

Options, roughly in order of effort:

1. Have the shared SSSOM write path stamp `mapping_date` (and bump
   `mapping_set_version`) whenever it writes rows. Needs a single choke point;
   there currently isn't one, which is the underlying problem.
2. Add it to `validate_sssom_invariants` as a warning: header date older than
   the file's last git-commit date.
3. Drop `mapping_set_version` and keep only `mapping_date`, stamped by a
   pre-commit hook.

Not blocking anything. Filing so it is not rediscovered a fourth time.
title: SSSOM mapping_set_version / mapping_date go stale — nothing bumps them

body:
Found in the review of the #299 revert (`87bd0aad`).

#299 was a published-identifier change that every gate passed. The revert fixes
those 64 subjects; it does not fix the reason nobody noticed.

## Why nothing saw it

- `validate_sssom_invariants` **Rule B1** lowercases the subject before matching
  it against `kgmicrobe.(ingredient|compound):<slug>`, so it is blind to subject
  case *by construction*. `test_registry_mint_is_invariant_to_subject_case` pins
  that property deliberately — it is correct, and it is the hole.
- **Rules A / B2 / B3** score the object label against the subject label. A
  subject slug rewrite does not touch either.
- `reconcile_sssom` checks GAP / ORPHAN / STALE against `ontology_id` and never
  reads the subject slug (already noted on #236).
- `check_flat_export_coverage` works from raw labels in `docs/data/`, not
  subjects.
- `audit_duplicate_identifiers` works on the record `identifier`, not the SSSOM
  subject.
- `check_sssom_subject_files` counts subjects with no matching file stem — and
  the mangling made that number go *down*, from 73 to 9. It scored the change as
  an improvement.

So the published surface of this project — the thing `docs/CURIE_STANDARD.md`
tells external consumers to persist — is the one thing no gate watches.

## What would catch it

The `qc-duplicate-ids` pattern, applied to subjects: commit a baseline of every
published `MIM:` subject, and fail when one disappears from it without an
accompanying row in `mappings/mim_curie_aliases.tsv`. Same shape as
`mappings/duplicate_identifier_baseline.tsv` — gate against *new* breakage
rather than assert a clean slate.

Sketch:

    scripts/audit_published_subjects.py --check      # exits 2
    mappings/published_mim_subjects_baseline.tsv     # subject_id, first_seen

Rules:
- subject in baseline, absent from SSSOM, no alias row -> **ERROR**
- subject in baseline, absent from SSSOM, alias row present -> OK
- subject in SSSOM, absent from baseline -> OK, `--apply` appends it

That also makes the alias map load-bearing instead of advisory. Today
`build_curie_alias_map` derives rows from git file renames under
`data/ingredients/` only, so a rename that touches the SSSOM and not the files
produces no alias and no complaint — which is precisely what happened.

## Interim coverage

`tests/test_published_mim_subject_case.py` pins the 64 subjects from #299 as a
literal table. That stops *this* regression recurring and nothing else. The next
published subject to move moves silently.

Related: #299, #236, #218 (the baseline pattern this would copy).
title: No gate catches a published MIM: subject leaving the mapping set

body:
**Found in review of #298. I consider this the blocking finding on that PR — it
is a published-identifier change, not a curation change, and it decides #236 by
side effect.**

Commit `988029fa` on `curation/edison-unmapped-sweep` realigned SSSOM subject IDs
to their per-record filenames. That was a genuine repair — subject/file drift went
from 75 unresolved to 9. But it renamed **62 already-published `MIM:` CURIEs**,
and the renaming rule lowercases everything after the first character, so acronyms
are mangled:

```
MIM:BG-11_Trace_Metals_Solution  ->  MIM:Bg-11_Trace_Metals_Solution
MIM:EDTA_Stock                   ->  MIM:Edta_Stock
MIM:MWC_Metal_Solution           ->  MIM:Mwc_Metal_Solution
MIM:P-IV_Metal_Solution          ->  MIM:P-iv_Metal_Solution
MIM:84_gL_NaHCO3_solution        ->  MIM:84_GL_NaHCO3_Solution
MIM:ATCC_Wolfes_mineral_mix      ->  MIM:Atcc_Wolfes_mineral_mix
```

Verified: 64 subjects on `main` are absent from the branch, 66 are new; folding
both sets to lowercase leaves a difference of exactly 2, which are the two records
promoted in that commit. So 62 are pure case changes.

Three problems.

**1. No alias trail is produced.** `scripts/build_curie_alias_map.py` derives
`mappings/mim_curie_aliases.tsv` from *git file renames* under `data/ingredients/`.
This commit renamed SSSOM subjects, not files, so no alias row is generated and
that TSV is unchanged. `docs/CURIE_STANDARD.md` lines 142-147 tell external
consumers to persist `MIM:<name>` and resolve through the alias map. These 62
become unresolvable with nothing pointing at the replacement.

**2. The new spellings are worse.** `MIM:Edta_Stock` and `MIM:P-iv_Metal_Solution`
are not improvements over `MIM:EDTA_Stock` and `MIM:P-IV_Metal_Solution`. If the
subject must match the filename, the argument runs at least as well in the other
direction — rename the files.

**3. It settles #236 by side effect.** #236 lists three options for subject/file
identity and is explicitly undecided. This picks option 3 (conform subjects to
filenames) inside a commit whose stated purpose was grounding two hydrates, with
no note in the message that 62 published identifiers moved.

No gate catches it: `validate_sssom_invariants.py` Rules A/B1/B2/B3 all pass,
because Rule B1 lowercases the subject before comparing and is therefore blind to
subject case entirely.

Options:

1. **Revert the subject renames**, keep the two groundings, and leave the drift
   at 75 until #236 is decided. Preserves every published CURIE.
2. **Keep them and emit alias rows**, teaching `build_curie_alias_map.py` to
   derive aliases from SSSOM subject history rather than only from file renames.
   Fixes resolution but keeps `MIM:Edta_Stock`.
